html:
The more than three and a half centuries, from 220 to 589, when China was split among rival states, between the fall of the Han and the reunification under the Sui.

It came in stages:

  • Three Kingdoms (220 to 280): Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the Han's remains, a time later made famous by the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
  • Jin (266 to 420): the Western Jin briefly reunited China in 280, then tore itself apart in the War of the Eight Princes. Northern peoples sacked Luoyang in 311, and many northern families fled south in the flight after Yongjia.
  • Sixteen Kingdoms and Northern and Southern dynasties (304 to 589): short-lived states, many led by non-Han peoples, ruled the north, while a chain of Han dynasties ruled the south from Jiankang, modern Nanjing.

The south is what "Six Dynasties" names: Wu, Eastern Jin, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen, all with their capital at Jiankang.

This was not a dark age. Buddhism spread widely, and the Northern Wei carved the Longmen Grottoes. The south developed its rice lands and became the richer half of China. The Northern Wei began the equal-field system of land allotment that the Sui and Tang kept. In 589 the Sui, a northern dynasty, conquered the Chen and joined China again.
sum: The more than three and a half centuries, from 220 to 589, when China was split among rival states, between the fall of the Han and the reunification under the Sui.
